content.text:
ANALYSIS ONLY — do not modify any file. Output prose, no patches.

Context (all verified against origin/main in this repo):
- Connectors return { events, checkpoint } only. They cannot emit entities or edges.
- `attributions` on a connector manifest eventKind resolve an event to entities and can auto-create them. See packages/connector-sdk/src/connector-types.ts:554-600 and packages/server/src/utils/entity-link-upsert.ts.
- `resolveLinksByKind` (entity-link-upsert.ts:734) already tracks matches keyed by rule AND by item index (`byRule`, `matchesByRule`), inside withEntityWriteTransaction.
- The connector sync path writes ZERO rows to `entity_relationships` today. The manifest has no `relationships` field.
- `entity_relationships` has a UNIQUE partial index on (from_entity_id,to_entity_id,relationship_type_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Columns: metadata jsonb, confidence, source, created_by, updated_by, deleted_at.
- `entity_relationship_types` has NO owner/system column; only nullable created_by (platform paths pass NULL) and a metadata jsonb.
- `member_of` is a live ACL gate (authz/channel-messages-visibility.ts:118). Lobu itself creates that type via ensureMemberOfType on any Slack/GitHub ACL sync, so it exists in an org WITHOUT anyone authoring it.
- Entity types and relationship types are owned by the org via `lobu apply`. DECIDED: connectors reference types by name, never create them.
- Today, if a referenced entity type is missing, auto-create logs a warning and returns null — silent no-op (entity-link-upsert.ts:490).
- Connectors will be written first-party, by customers using their own coding agents, and eventually some publicly exposed.
- Target use case: an ERP (invoices, customers). An invoice event names its customer; we want an invoice->customer edge.

Give me a direct opinion on EACH decision below. For each: your recommendation, the strongest argument AGAINST your recommendation, and any failure mode you think we have not considered. Be blunt; disagree with me where warranted. Prioritise correctness and DX for a connector author who is an AI agent writing a manifest.

D1. Manifest shape. Option A: add `name?: string` to EventAttributionRule, plus `relationships: [{ type, from: <attrName>, to: <attrName> }]` on the eventKind. Option B: express it inline on the attribution rule (e.g. `relatesTo: { type, attribution }`). Option C: something else you prefer.

D2. Missing relationship type in the org. Option A: hard-fail the whole sync run. Option B: skip that edge, continue, and surface a setup task/notification to the org. Option C: keep today's silent warn.

D3. Protecting ACL-bearing types. Option A: stamp platform-created relationship types (metadata.owner='system') and refuse connector assertion of those. Option B: hardcoded slug deny-list. Option C: allow, gate later at install-consent.

D4. Retraction. If an invoice's customer changes, the old edge must go. Who reconciles, and how does a connector express "this event's edges are the complete set for this subject"? Consider that events are append-only and a resync mints new event rows.

D5. Cardinality. An invoice belongs to exactly one customer. Enforce at write time, or detect after the fact? Note every existing edge type in this repo (member_of, about, mentions) is naturally many-to-many.

D6. Provenance. We want to be able to answer "which connector/rule asserted this edge" and "retract everything connector X asserted". There is a partial index on metadata->'derivedFrom'->>'relationshipTypeId' and ->>'ruleVersion' but it carries no org, connection, or rule name. events.id is a stored-version id that changes on resync, so it is NOT a stable provenance key. What should we key on?

I’m using the Lobu operator guidance because this is a repo-contract/design review. I’ll inspect the exact manifest, transaction, ACL, and schema paths read-only, plus the relevant prior design notes, then give a blunt D1–D6 verdict without modifying anything.

The core fault line is already clear: a relationship edge is not the same thing as a connector assertion. The current live-triple uniqueness collapses identical edges from multiple producers, so provenance and safe retraction cannot both be correct if they are stored as one scalar `source`/`derivedFrom` record. I’m tracing the sync transaction and ACL writers now to pin down the least dangerous contract.

My overall view: do not model this as “connectors create edges.” Model it as “connectors make versioned, retractable assertions; the server materializes the live edge graph.” Without that distinction, D4 and D6 cannot be made correct under multiple connectors.

## D1 — Manifest shape

**Recommendation: modified Option A / Option C.** Keep relationships separate from attributions, but use stable machine keys, not optional names.

Add an additive `key?: string` to `EventAttributionRule`; require it whenever a relationship references that attribution. Add event-kind relationships shaped conceptually as: stable relationship `key`, relationship type slug, `from` attribution key, `to` attribution key, and explicit reconciliation mode.

`name` is the wrong word. Everywhere else it implies a human-facing label that authors may freely rename. Provenance and retraction need an immutable identifier. The relationship itself also needs a stable key; endpoint names alone do not identify the rule across manifest versions.

Option B is worse. Inline `relatesTo` makes one endpoint structurally privileged, makes reuse awkward, and still needs a forward reference. One attribution may participate in several edges, so relationships are naturally peer declarations over named resolved values.

The strongest argument against separate relationships is verbosity: an AI author must name two attributions and then join them. That is real, but it buys deterministic validation and provenance. Good diagnostics can make the error actionable: duplicate key, unknown endpoint, missing type, or prohibited type.

Failure modes:

- The existing per-item return value loses rule identity—it is just `number[]`. Relationship resolution needs an `item index × attribution key → entity ID` result. The existing `byRule` and indexed entries make this a straightforward extension without re-resolving identities.
- Missing, null, ambiguous, and explicitly empty endpoints must not collapse into one state. An unresolved identity is an error; it must not be interpreted as “the complete desired edge set is empty.”
- Relationship-rule key removal or rename must retract the old rule’s assertions during connector-definition reconciliation. A rule version/hash is not a stable key.
- Validate relationship keys, attribution references, relationship types, endpoint type-pair rules, and protected types before a sync starts.

The published SDK contract should remain additive: `key` can be optional for legacy attribution-only manifests, but conditionally mandatory when referenced by `relationships`.

## D2 — Missing relationship type

**Recommendation: Option A, plus the setup task from B.** Fail the run and surface an actionable setup notification. Do not skip the edge and advance the checkpoint.

A relationship declaration is part of the connector’s declared output contract. Persisting the invoice event while silently omitting its customer edge creates a valid-looking but semantically incomplete workspace. For an incremental connector, the invoice may never be emitted again, so Option B creates a permanent hole unless you also build a durable event-reprojection mechanism.

The best DX is to catch this before dispatch: connection/feed activation should enter `setup_required` with the exact missing type and expected endpoint types. Runtime lookup must still fail closed because schemas can drift after validation. A relationship-bound attribution whose entity type is missing should also become strict; keeping today’s warning/no-op there would merely move the silent failure one step earlier.

The strongest argument against A is availability: an optional graph feature can stop useful raw ingestion. That is especially painful for public connectors installed into arbitrary organizations. The answer is preflight and setup UX, not corrupted partial output. If you later introduce an explicitly best-effort relationship mode backed by replayable stored events, that can opt into skipping. It should not be the default.

Unconsidered failure: “fail the whole run” is not currently equivalent to transactional rollback. The real sync path commits streamed batches and events incrementally. A late failure can leave earlier batches committed. Preflight is therefore load-bearing; true whole-run atomicity would require staging/generation semantics. At runtime, at minimum, fail the current item/batch and never advance its checkpoint.

## D3 — ACL-bearing relationship types

**Recommendation: none of A–C is sufficient alone. Use B as the immediate safety gate, then introduce a first-class, non-user-settable authorization classification.**

Immediately reject connector assertions for every relationship type consumed by authz, using one centralized registry shared by the ACL readers and connector writer. Do not rely on install consent. A connector that can mint `member_of` can mint authorization, and ordinary “read ERP data” consent is not an adequate privilege boundary.

For the durable design, use a real `purpose = 'authorization'` or equivalent system-controlled classification—preferably a column, or protected metadata as an interim—and make both sides depend on it:

- ACL queries only trust relationship types marked authorization-bearing.
- The connector assertion chokepoint categorically refuses those types.

`metadata.owner='system'` alone is too broad and too easy to forget. System-created `mentions` is not equivalent to authorization. More importantly, if ACL reads continue trusting the slug alone, forgetting to stamp one future type produces a security hole. If the read itself requires the classification, forgetting the marker fails closed.

The strongest argument against a hardcoded deny-list is drift and namespace capture. The repo already uses `member_of` as both a general domain term and an ACL primitive. Blocking it prevents legitimate domain modeling, while allowing it permits privilege escalation. Long term, ACL should use a reserved type such as `$acl_member_of`, or ideally a separate authorization graph.

The particularly nasty existing failure is that `ensureMemberOfType` adopts any active org-local `member_of` row through `ON CONFLICT`, while authz checks only the slug. There is no reliable historical distinction between “platform-created” and “preexisting org type.” A migration must classify/adopt all current ACL incarnations deliberately; checking nullable `created_by` is not sufficient.

Option C is a hard no. Consent is defense in depth, not the enforcement boundary for authorization writes.

## D4 — Retraction

**Recommendation: the server reconciles; the connector declares whether each relationship rule is authoritative.**

Give each relationship rule an explicit mode such as `reconcile: 'replace'`. For each event item, that means: “for this stable source subject and this stable relationship rule, these resolved edges are the complete desired set.”

The reconciliation scope should be based on stable source identity:

`organization + connection + origin_id + relationship_rule_key`

Include connector key for audit/filtering, but do not use `events.id`. A superseding event version has the same source subject and replaces the previous desired assertion set.

The write flow should be:

1. Resolve named attributions for the item.
2. Persist or find the current event version under the existing `(connection_id, origin_id)` serialization.
3. In that same `insertEvent` transaction/hook, upsert the desired assertions and deactivate this scope’s obsolete assertions.
4. Materialize or retract the live edge according to whether any active assertion still supports it.

That shared event-write boundary is important: `afterPersist` runs for inserted, superseded, and unchanged events, so a manifest/rule change can reproject an unchanged source item. Writing edges earlier in the current attribution transaction could leave an edge committed when the later event insert fails.

The strongest argument against server reconciliation is that the server cannot know whether a connector emitted a complete object or a partial patch. Correct—which is why `replace` must be explicit, not inferred. Append-only/inferred rules can use a different mode.

Failure modes:

- Distinguish an absent field from explicit `null`. For a `0..1` relationship, explicit null may mean clear; omitted data may mean partial payload and must not retract.
- For exactly-one, an unresolved or missing customer is an error, not an empty replacement set.
- A source deletion requires either a tombstone/update with the same `origin_id` and an empty desired set, or a separate full-feed snapshot protocol. Incremental silence cannot prove deletion.
- Never reconcile globally from one batch. Batches and pages are partial; reconcile only subjects actually observed.
- Rule removal, connector uninstall, and connection deletion need lifecycle-driven assertion retraction even if the source item never appears again.

## D5 — Cardinality

**Recommendation: enforce at write time. Detection afterward is monitoring, not correctness.**

Cardinality belongs to the org-owned relationship-type schema, not the connector manifest. Otherwise two connectors can reference the same type while declaring incompatible semantics. Extend the relationship type’s allowed source/target rules with unambiguous constraints such as `minTargetsPerSource` and `maxTargetsPerSource`. Existing types default to unbounded many-to-many.

For invoice → customer, `maxTargetsPerSource = 1`; if the domain truly requires a customer, `minTargetsPerSource = 1` is checked at the authoritative event boundary. Updating customer A to B must retract A and assert B atomically.

The write kernel must serialize competing writes for the same source entity/type—via ordered entity locks or another Postgres-mediated lock—and every writer must pass through it. A post-insert query that discovers two customers has already exposed an invalid graph. The current live-triple index only prevents the exact same edge twice; it does not prevent invoice → customer A and invoice → customer B.

The strongest argument against strict write-time enforcement is eventual consistency: partial ERP payloads, overlapping runs, or two producers may temporarily disagree. That is why minimum cardinality should apply only to explicitly authoritative snapshots. Maximum cardinality still must be enforced before making the conflicting edge live.

Unconsidered failure: two independent producers can assert different customers for the same exact-one invoice. Do not silently choose the latest or overwrite the other producer. Reject/quarantine the conflicting assertion and surface it. Manual assertions participate in the same conflict; connector reconciliation must never erase them.

## D6 — Provenance

**Recommendation: add a normalized relationship-assertion ledger. Do not put one `derivedFrom` object on the edge and call it done.**

The live edge and the assertion supporting it have different identity. Because the current unique index collapses all identical live triples, two connectors asserting the same edge cannot be represented as two `entity_relationships` rows. Conversely, storing only one producer in edge metadata means retracting connector X can incorrectly delete an edge still asserted by connector Y or a human.

Each assertion needs two keys:

The stable ownership/reconciliation scope:

`organization_id, producer_kind, connector_key, connection_id, origin_id, relationship_rule_key`

The claimed edge member:

`relationship_type_id, from_entity_id, to_entity_id`

Store `feed_key`, event kind, connector-definition version, manifest/rule version or hash, run ID, and the most recent stored event ID as audit evidence. They are not ownership identity. In particular, the stored event ID is useful for “which version most recently observed this?” but must never drive retraction.

Index active assertions by exact reconciliation scope and separately by `(organization_id, connector_key, connection_id)` for bulk teardown. Then:

- “Which connector/rule asserted this edge?” reads its active assertions.
- “Retract connection X” deactivates assertions by connection.
- “Retract every installation of connector X in this org” filters by org and connector key.
- The live edge is soft-deleted only when its last active assertion disappears.

The existing JSON expression index on relationship type/rule version is inadequate: rule version is deliberately unstable, and it lacks connection, source subject, and rule identity. An array of assertions inside edge metadata looks cheaper but creates lost-update races, awkward indexing, and painful entity-merge handling.

The strongest argument against an assertion table is complexity: another lifecycle, migration, materialization step, and entity-merge integration. But that complexity already exists in the domain. Keeping it implicit in mutable JSON does not remove it; it makes retraction nondeterministic.

Additional failure modes include entity merges needing to repoint and coalesce assertions, relationship-type archive/recreation producing a new type incarnation, rule-key renames orphaning old scopes, and confidence/metadata conflicts between multiple producers.

Bottom line: D1 modified A, D2 A with setup UX, D3 immediate deny-list plus a real ACL classification, D4 server-owned replace reconciliation, D5 write-time enforcement, and D6 a separate assertion ledger. I would not add direct connector inserts into `entity_relationships` before the assertion/reconciliation boundary exists.

No files were modified.
